brand.text:
## What the customer actually buys

Orbital Foundry builds furniture and interior fittings for ships, orbital stations and colonies. The customer does not buy a sofa first. They buy a fitting that survives a hard dock, works in partial gravity and still looks like home after five years of recycled air.

Practical rule: **a material name is never a promise.** "Titanium frame" describes a part. The promise is what stops happening: a chair that no longer rattles when the station spins up.

## Mechanism

Every product goes through the vacuum test bench before it leaves the Foundry, and the test result ships with it. The customer buys a measured result, not a declaration of quality. Say the mechanism early, not in the small print.

## Differentiators

Every sales text stands on at least one of them. A text that stands on none describes the furniture trade, not us.

1. **Tested, not claimed.** Each piece is vacuum-tested and certified for artificial gravity; the test card travels with the order.
2. **Built to be repaired on board.** Standard fasteners, spare parts listed per product, no glued joints in load-bearing parts.
3. **Designed for small cabins.** Every collection has a fold, stack or wall-mount variant for crew quarters.

## AI

We use automation to write first drafts of catalogue texts. It is a way of working, not a product. We never sell "AI furniture".

They have been burned by furniture that looked good in a render and came apart in the first gravity cycle. They believe specifications more than adjectives and expect to be told when a product is the wrong choice.

personas.text: Buys for a whole deck at once. Cares about lead time, spare parts and how many pieces fit in one cargo pod. Reads the specification table before the description.

personas.text: Furnishes one cabin for a two-year contract. Cares about comfort in low gravity, noise and whether the piece folds away. Skims; decides on the first two sentences.

personas.name: Colony homesteader
personas.text: Furnishes a first permanent home. Cares about durability and repair on site, distrusts anything that needs a service technician.

tone.text:
Three rules, each with a test. Not nine adjectives: an adjective has no pass criterion.

## Rule 1: practitioner to practitioner

Write like someone who has fitted a cabin, to someone who is fitting one.

Test: read it aloud. A sentence you would not say to a customer at the dock gets rewritten until you would.

- DO: "The Docking Bay Chair locks to the floor rail in two clicks, so it stays put during a hard burn."
- DON'T: "Our extensive experience allows us to deliver exceptional seating solutions."

## Rule 2: a specific instead of an adjective

Test: swap our name for a competitor's. If the sentence is still true, cut it.

- DO: "The frame is tested for 500 vacuum cycles."
- DON'T: "Premium quality and outstanding durability."

## Rule 3: warm in voice, firm in promise

Speak directly, use "you". What we promise is hard: measurements, test results, warranty terms.

Active voice, first person plural: we test, we ship, we repair. Not "is tested by".

## Zero is a valid result

No good FAQ question? Zero questions is correct. No number in the facts registry? The sentence goes without a number or not at all. Filler looks useful and is not.
ai_patterns: Contrast for show: "it's not X, it's Y" and its relatives.
Forced triplets: three adjectives or three clauses only because three sounds good.
Symmetric sentences and paragraphs of the same length.
Warm-up openers: "in today's world", "in an era of", "more and more".
Process narration: "in this article", "let's dive in", "our first step".
An aphorism closing every section; at most two per text.
The long dash; use a short dash with spaces or a comma.

language.text:
## Names

- **Orbital Foundry**: two words, both capitalised, never shortened to "OF" in customer texts.
- Collection names are proper names: "Orion Collection", "Nebula Heritage". Never translated.

## Dashes

| Mark | When |
|---|---|
| Hyphen `-` without spaces | joining words: `low-gravity cabin` |
| Dash `-` with spaces | an aside |
| Long dash `—` | never |
| En dash `–` | numeric ranges only: `0.3–1.2 g` |

## Banned phrases

| Phrase | Instead |
|---|---|
| state-of-the-art | name the part or the test |
| game-changing | say what changes |
| one-stop solution | list what is included |
| world-class | give a number from the facts registry |
| revolutionise your cabin | say what will be different |

## Capitals

Headings in sentence case. Not Every Word Capitalised.

headlines.text:
A headline names the reader's situation or shows the mechanism. It never praises us.

- DO: "A desk that stays put when the station spins up"
- DON'T: "Discover our amazing new desk"

A call to action is a verb and an object: "Check dimensions", "Order spare parts". One primary call per page.

proof.text:
Proof is a number from the facts registry, a test result or a named collection. Read this before deciding to put a proof in a text, not after.

- A number goes in only if it is in the facts registry and verified.
- Numbers from others (industry reports) go in only with the source named in the same sentence.
- No invented customer quotes, no invented reviews, no "thousands of happy crews".

seo.text:
Intent first, volume second: pick the phrase whose results page shows texts of the same type as ours.

- Exactly one H1; sections as H2, subsections as H3, no skipped levels.
- Each main section answers its question in the first 40-60 words.
- Primary phrase in the H1 and the lead; each secondary phrase in at least one heading or the first sentence of its section, never stuffed.
- Meta title 40-60 characters, primary phrase near the start, not a copy of the H1. Meta description 140-160 characters, with a concrete benefit.
- Image alt text describes what the image shows, in natural language.

checklists.text:
Only checkable items. An item you cannot verify in a few seconds is a wish, not a check.

## Every text

- [ ] No long dash. Check with search, not by eye.
- [ ] "Orbital Foundry" spelled as two capitalised words.
- [ ] Every number comes from the facts registry.
- [ ] No phrase from the banned list.
- [ ] No "it's not X, it's Y" construction.
- [ ] Sentences vary in length.
- [ ] Swap test: no sentence about us stays true with a competitor's name.

## Product description

- [ ] Opens with the main benefit in one sentence.
- [ ] Every specification comes from the product data.
- [ ] Says when the product is the wrong choice, if the data supports it.

## Article

- [ ] Each section answers its question in the first 40-60 words.
- [ ] Every factual sentence has a source in the brief, the answers or the facts registry.
- [ ] FAQ has 0-6 questions; zero is fine.
